items.t: BARC: Buybacks Matter More, Mixed Execution Leaves The Upside Intact
sum: Barclays' updated analyst price target edges down by £0.13, reflecting slightly lower fair value, modestly adjusted revenue growth and profit margin assumptions, and updated P/E expectations following recent Street research that cited mixed quarterly results and only minor forecast changes.

Recent Street research on Barclays points to a more balanced view from analysts, with several price target cuts but differing opinions on how attractive the stock looks at current levels. The focus is on how recent quarterly execution, capital returns and revised P/E assumptions compare with the updated fair value range.
- Some bullish analysts see scope for shareholder returns to play a bigger role in the investment case, with higher buyback estimates helping support the valuation even as price targets move lower.

- JPMorgan keeps an Overweight rating alongside its reduced 580 GBp target, which indicates that at least one major bank still views Barclays as offering upside potential relative to its own fair value work.
- Minor forecast changes in recent notes suggest that, while expectations have been adjusted, analysts are not radically reworking revenue or profit margin assumptions for Barclays at this stage.

- Price targets in the 540 GBp to 580 GBp range indicate that some analysts still see room between current trading levels and their view of fair value, subject to execution on earnings and capital return plans.
- All three recent research updates lowered price targets, which shows that analysts are marking down their assessment of fair value for Barclays rather than lifting it.

Bloom Energy Lands Barclays Upgrade as Google and NTT DATA Deals Put Fuel Cells at the Heart of AI P
sum: Bloom Energy shares climbed 4.1% on Wednesday, riding a broader rebound in technology and growth stocks as investors shifted attention back to the company's fuel-cell projects with Google and NTT DATA. The advance came a day after Barclays lifted its rating on the stock from "Equal-Weight" to "Overweight," even as analyst Christine Cho trimmed her price target to $289 from $316. Cho pointed to demand that is gathering pace faster than anticipated — an upgrade in sentiment that, notably, arrived without a corresponding increase in the target price.

The rally followed a rough session for companies tied to data-center buildouts. Reuters reported a wide selloff in technology and AI-related names as investors reassessed what the previous day's Democratic midterm victories might mean for the pace of AI infrastructure spending. Bloom was caught in that downdraft before recovering.

The catalyst investors are watching most closely is Google's announcement of a $17 billion data center in Wyoming, part of whose power supply is slated to come from a fuel-cell installation Bloom is expected to equip. The project calls for 702 megawatts of fuel-cell capacity and includes CO? capture and storage — a combination that pairs electricity for the campus with a planned method for handling its emissions. Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and Related Digital round out the partner list.

That pairing of power supply and carbon management sits at the center of the Bloom thesis. Its fuel cells run mainly on natural gas and generate electricity without combustion; adding carbon capture to the Wyoming project would extend that model to the emissions side of the equation. The opportunity is real, provided the plans turn into built plants.

The same caveat applies to a partnership reported Wednesday with California Resource Corporation and Carbon TerraVault. The companies will study power-generation projects with CO? capture exceeding 1 GW. For Bloom, it is another route to linking its fuel cells with emissions handling — but the arrangement is non-binding, which makes execution, not intention, the measure that matters. Firm project commitments now carry more weight than announcements.

Bloom Energy Rallies as Barclays Turns Bullish, but California Carbon Pact Remains a Blueprint
sum: Bloom Energy shares climbed 7.2% on Tuesday, extending a rally set in motion a day earlier when Barclays lifted its rating on the fuel-cell maker and the company unveiled a preliminary carbon-capture partnership in California. Monday's session had already delivered a 9.1% advance, with media reports pointing to the same two catalysts behind both moves.

The Barclays note moved Bloom to Overweight from Equal Weight, with analyst Christine Cho citing faster-than-expected demand, rising customer down payments and new delivery commitments. Yet the bank trimmed its price target to $289 from $316 — a reminder that a more favourable rating does not automatically translate into a higher valuation benchmark.

Separately, director John T. Chambers offloaded 8,828 shares on Monday at a weighted average price of $203.43, according to a mandatory filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. The transaction was executed under a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan adopted on 26 February, a structure that fixes sales in advance and shields insiders from timing allegations.

Ownership disclosures also shifted. Vanguard Capital Management reported an economically attributable stake of 7.39% in a Schedule 13G filed on 30 October, with the filing naming 30 September as the event date.

The non-binding letter of intent with California Resources Corporation and its unit Carbon TerraVault covers a feasibility review of at least 1 GW of fuel-cell capacity, to be paired with carbon capture and storage in California. According to Data Center Dynamics, the concept could eventually capture and store up to 3 million tonnes of CO? annually. Both figures describe the project's potential, not capacity already in place.

Utilities, data centres and industrial customers are named as possible offtakers. The appeal of the arrangement lies in treating power supply and carbon management as a single package rather than two separate ventures — a route that could take Bloom beyond the economics of an individual fuel-cell installation. Whether that becomes a durable business depends on more than the technical concept.
California Resources Corporation has stressed that the plan hinges on definitive agreements, financing, required permits and further consents.

Commerzbank: 21.27 Million Shares Retired as Buyback Outpaces Barclays' Downgrade
sum: Commerzbank has repurchased 21,268,730 of its own shares since launching the current buyback programme on 4 September, the lender disclosed on Monday. The tally, which runs through Friday, confirms the bank is still executing the plan rather than merely talking about it — a distinction that matters with third-quarter figures due on 5 November.

The most recent weekly report covers 26 to 30 October, during which 3,316,027 shares were bought back. That pace is slower than the 3,681,593 shares reported for the prior week on 26 October. Neither figure says anything about an expansion or a conclusion of the programme; they simply track how much of the existing mandate has been carried out.

Buybacks of this kind speak to how Commerzbank is deploying capital. They do not answer the question investors are really asking, which is whether the core business can stand on its own. That makes the 5 November release the more consequential date on the calendar, with the analyst call set for 09:00 and the press conference at 10:30.

Sentiment around the standalone case took a knock on 22 October, when Barclays analyst Paola Sabbione cut her price target to 41 euros and downgraded the stock from "Overweight" to "Equal Weight." The move is a counterweight to any thesis built purely on takeover speculation — though it is no forecast for the upcoming report.

Separately, the ECB last week trimmed the additional Pillar 2 capital requirement (P2R) for 2027 by 5 basis points to 2.10% of total capital. Commerzbank puts its pro-forma MDA threshold for hard core capital at 10.26% of risk-weighted assets. Lower capital requirements are not the same as higher earnings, and no fresh buyback commitment can be inferred from the combination.

On the operational side, ver.di has called employees at private banks, Commerzbank included, to regional warning strikes, with collective bargaining talks due to resume in Frankfurt on Monday. No earnings impact can be quantified from the walkout, and neither can any effect on day-to-day operations — but the dispute sharpens the question of how well the business absorbs extra costs.
The takeover question remains open. According to Reuters, UniCredit said on Friday it would keep financing German mid-sized companies even in the event of a possible acquisition.

Siemens Energy: Barclays Flags a Margin Ceiling as a 6.1% AI Slide Puts 11 November in the Spotlight
sum: Siemens Energy shares fell 6.1% on Friday, caught in a widening pullback from artificial intelligence names. For investors, the sell-off raises a question that has less to do with the share price than with the business behind it: can the company still justify expectations built on higher prices and wider margins, or do those forecasts now need trimming?

According to dpa-AFX, doubts about the profitability of multi-billion-dollar AI investments weighed on Siemens Energy alongside its peers. Media reports pointed to Intel's weaker quarterly outlook as an additional drag on AI-linked stocks. The decline is therefore best read as a reaction to the broader market backdrop rather than to any new guidance from Siemens Energy itself.

That distinction matters. A sector-wide loss of confidence can hit companies whose own expectations are unchanged — but it can equally expose assumptions that had gone unchallenged. The price move alone does not settle which reading applies.

The more specific pressure came from Barclays, which according to media reports warned of limited room for further price and margin increases in the energy technology sector. The scepticism is thus not confined to the scale of future data-centre spending. It extends to how much economic benefit suppliers can actually extract from it.

For Siemens Energy shareholders, demand and earnings quality are two separate things. Even if investment keeps flowing, the terms available to equipment makers remain an open question. The risk therefore lies not only in possible project cuts but in assumptions about profitability that may prove too optimistic.

Comments on pricing and margins will carry particular weight at the next set of results. Hard evidence could help separate industry-wide caution from the company's own trajectory. General confidence about demand, by contrast, would not fully answer the concern about a margin ceiling.

The company's ongoing share repurchase belongs in the same assessment. Siemens Energy reported the acquisition of 1,294,334 of its own shares in its latest interim disclosure, covering the period from 19 to 25 October. In total, 4,513,232 shares had been bought back under the programme by that point.

Coinbase Shares Plunge to 2-Year Low as Bitcoin Slides Under $77K and Barclays, JPMorgan Slash Targets
sum: Coinbase Global Inc (COIN) fell more than 13% in morning trading Friday to its weakest level since February 2024, as a sharp selloff in Bitcoin dragged crypto-linked equities lower and a wave of Wall Street desks trimmed their price targets on the exchange following third-quarter results.

The stock touched lows not seen in more than two years. Bitcoin (BTC) slid as much as 5.5% over 24 hours to trade near $77,000, adding fresh pressure to a sector already rattled by turmoil at rival exchange Binance.

Coinbase's quarter was a split verdict. The company reported earnings of $2.51 per share, far ahead of the $0.08 consensus tracked by Koyfin, but revenue of $1.21 billion came in just below the $1.22 billion analysts had expected.

Barclays cut its target to $120 from $149 while keeping an Underweight rating, warning that a lower revenue run rate heading into the fourth quarter and higher-than-expected costs would force a "sizeable downgrade" to near-term EBITDA estimates.

JPMorgan's Kenneth Worthington said the transaction environment remained difficult and that assigning value to Coinbase's growing prediction-markets business was a challenge. Wells Fargo, meanwhile, credited prediction markets and the USDC stablecoin with cushioning the weak crypto backdrop, though it said the quarter offered little sign of a broader acceleration.

Needham lowered its target to $197 from $205 while maintaining a Buy rating, pointing to the Binance developments as a source of market turbulence that coincided with Coinbase's report. The firm also flagged AI-driven hacking risk as a mounting concern for the sector through 2027.
Note: Target figures reflect the most recent revisions reported around Coinbase's third-quarter results. Ratings were maintained at prior levels across the desks listed.

sum: Investing.com -- Barclays downgraded airport operator Fraport to "underweight" from "equal weight" on Tuesday, citing weaker winter traffic, and cut its price target to €57 from €68.

It also downgraded Athens International Airport to "underweight" from "equal weight", while raising its price target to €10.95 from €10.70 =. Barclays said the stock's recent strength, which it suspects was driven by index buying, has left it overvalued.

Athens shares have risen about 20% since Sept. 1, while the Stoxx 600 has fallen about 2.5%, Barclays said, leaving about 10% downside to its raised target. The higher target reflects a cut in its cost of equity to 7.6% from 7.9% after Greece was upgraded from emerging to developed market status.

Athens is also bidding for a 40-year concession covering 22 regional Greek airports serving a combined 2.4 million passengers. Barclays said the outcome is uncertain and does not materially change its near-term earnings outlook.

Barclays expects airlines to reduce capacity plans this winter unless fuel prices fall back sharply. It noted that airBaltic, Volotea and AnimaWings have filed for bankruptcy protection in recent weeks and expects other small airlines to follow.

For Fraport, Barclays forecast third-quarter underlying EBITDA of €553 million =, 8% below Bloomberg consensus. It raised its labour-cost assumptions to account for a favourable one-off in the year-earlier comparison.
It cut its 2026 and 2027 Frankfurt passenger forecasts to 63.0 million and 65.3 million from 63.2 million and 66.5 million, respectively.

As Lloyds shares stumble, is that dividend yield safe?
sum: Lloyds‘ (LSE: LLOY) share price has stumbled, falling 5% in the last month. That’s nothing to panic about. Lloyds’ shares are still up 30% over one year and 147% over five. Plus some juicy dividends on top.
Recent weakness reflects wider economic concerns rather than anything going badly wrong at the FTSE 100 bank. After a terrific run for the sector, some investors may simply be taking profits.

But things could get bumpier as unemployment, food prices, energy bills and mortgage rates rise, squeezing consumers and businesses. As a Lloyds’ shareholder, I’m expecting the shares to slow. These things go in cycles. But I’m curious about the dividend. Can it keep growing?

Right now, things look good. Lloyds has increased its ordinary dividend by roughly 15% a year for the last three years. The total full-year payout has climbed from 2.76p per share in 2023 to 3.17p in 2024 and 3.65p in 2025. The board recently increased the 2026 interim dividend by an even more impressive 30% to 1.58p.

With the shares at around 110p, the trailing yield’s 3.3%. The forecast 2026 dividend of about 4.01p gives a prospective yield of around 3.6%. That isn’t spectacular compared with some of my FTSE dividend income favourites, but it’s partly down to the fact that Lloyds’ shares have gone gangbusters.
So what about dividend cover? Pretty good actually. It generated 7p of earnings per share in 2025 against a 3.65p ordinary dividend, giving cover of almost two times.
The first half of 2026 showed the bank’s still making bags of money. Statutory profit after tax rose 23% to £3.1bn, while net income increased 9% to £9.7bn. Return on tangible equity reached 17.1%.

Which now offer better value: NatWest or Barclays shares?
sum: Barclays' (LSE: BARC) shares have had a brilliant run, soaring 170% in five years. But they've been beaten by rival FTSE 100 bank NatWest (LSE: NWG). It's up a staggering 225%.

Their performances have been driven by rising interest rates, which allowed them to widen net interest margins and increase profits. So investors have started seriously looking at UK banking stocks again, both for share price growth and dividend income. But which bank is more tempting?
My first question is a wider one. Can the good times continue as the economy gets bumpier?
At the start of the year, interest rates were widely expected to fall. Because of the Iran war, that hasn't happened. Instead, markets are pricing in four UK base rate hikes next year.
That should support net interest margins, but there's a catch. The slowing economy could reduce demand for mortgages and savings products, while pushing debt impairments higher.

Barclays and NatWest face political risk too, with speculation about a windfall tax in the Autumn Budget. Another worry is that after such a strong share price performance, gravity may naturally assert itself.

NatWest's latest results were impressive. First-half operating profit rose 20.4% to £4.32bn, while income increased 11% to £8.86bn. Net interest margins edged higher, reaching 2.49% in the second quarter.

Barclays falls despite lifting income target and unveiling larger buyback - UPDATE
sum: Barclays PLC (LSE:BARC) shares fell 5.1% to 503p despite the bank upgrading its 2026 income target and announcing a £1 billion share buyback after stronger investment banking and interest income lifted second-quarter profit.

The FTSE 100 lender reported group income of £8.3 billion in the second quarter, up 16% on a year ago, while pre-tax profit rose 31% to £3.3 billion. Return on tangible equity in the quarter improved to 16.1% from 12.3% a year earlier and 13.5% in Q1.

Investment banking revenue rose 20% to £3.96 billion, beating the £3.66 billion City consensus, as global markets income and advisory fees increased. Fixed-income, currencies and commodities revenue of £1.47 billion fell slightly short of the £1.51 billion forecast.
UK lending balances grew 5% year on year, as mortgage margin pressure partly offset higher structural hedge income at Barclays UK. UK's net interest margin widened to 3.70% from 3.55% a year earlier.

The bank increased its 2026 group income target to around £31.5 billion from £31 billion. Guidance for net interest income excluding the investment bank and head office was raised to more than £13.7 billion from more than £13.5 billion.

Barclays maintained its forecast for full-year return on tangible equity above 12%. It expects its loan-loss rate near the top of its 0.5% to 0.6% range after impairment charges increased to £600 million in the quarter.
Chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said Barclays had delivered "another strong quarter", supported by UK lending growth and the investment bank performing well "in a favourable environment".

After it rocketed to a 19-year high, here’s what the experts say about the Barclays share price outlook…
sum: At 536p, the Barclays (LSE: BARC) share price is now at its highest since November 2007, almost two decades ago.
That’s an astonishing figure and reflects the damage done by the financial crisis, which saw the share price crash from 665p in January 2007 to less than a pound in two years.
Barclays shares bumped along the bottom for an age before finally getting their mojo back three years ago. They’ve rocketed 250% since August 2023, with dividends on top. So what’s been driving them?

Like all the banks, the Barclays bottom line has been boosted by higher interest rates, which allows it to widen net interest margins, the difference between what it pays savers and charges borrowers. Management has also integrated the acquisition of Tesco Bank nicely, while structural hedge income has further driven revenues.

Barclays also posted a 10.5% return on tangible equity (RoTE) figure in 2024 and 11.3% in 2025, boosted by record investment banking income. It’s aiming for 14% by 2028. Pre-tax group profits have been flying, as this table shows:
The board has also been rewarding investors with both dividends and share buybacks, as part of a multi-year plan to return more than £15bn to shareholders by 2028.

Despite all that, the shares still look decent value with a forward price-to-earnings ratio of just 10. The 2.88% forecast yield for 2026 is a little low, but that’s because the board plans to reward investors primarily through share buybacks. That’s worth bearing in mind if dividends are your priority. The anticipated yield for 2027 is 3.56%, so it’s not too meagre.
